notes.key_messages: To gain high marks for a coursework assignment, a candidate should: ● ensure the assignment title is a question which requires investigation ● ensure the question is an analytical question rather than a descriptive question ● use both primary and secondary research to gather information relevant to the question and then analyse this information ● ensure that the assignment ends with a conclusion which answers the question posed in the title and is based on the information gathered.
notes.general_comments: The coursework option was mainly undertaken by Centres that had previously entered candidates but there were also a number of new ones too. A few popular sections of the syllabus continue to be favoured by candidates for their coursework. Overall the standard of work submitted was high, with very few low-scoring pieces of coursework. Assessment criteria Questionnaires continued to be the most popular form of primary research for the majority of candidates. Sources of information selected by candidates included visits to businesses; interviews (with parents, business people, and the general public); the Internet, and also information such as advertisements, maps and photographs. Some candidates discussed their approach to the research – who, when, why and how it was carried out – which was helpful, often contributing to their gaining higher marks for Assessment Objective 2. In addition, textbooks were also used to provide an explanation of business concepts and terminology applied to research findings. Assignment titles were usually analytical and encouraged a wide range of research. Occasionally titles were descriptive, such as ‘How does XYZ company motivate its staff?’ They often still encouraged a wide range of research to be undertaken by the candidate. However, their analysis and evaluation of this information was often lacking detail and consequently this resulted in lower marks than they might have gained if a different title had been set. Better candidates posed themselves an analytical question (e.g. ‘How well does XYZ company motivate its staff?’), which they answered in the conclusion and so gained higher marks for Assessment Objective 4. Candidates made effective use of IT to present their coursework. The majority of candidates presented their findings in a logical manner with a clear title, outline of the problem/question set, research findings with analysis of the data and ending with a conclusion that answered the question posed in the title. Application of the assessment criteria The assessment criteria were accurately applied by the majority of Centres and this was a reflection of their experience in assessing coursework. Very occasionally Centres were slightly generous and this was usually in the awarding of analysis and evaluation marks. Where discussion by candidates was brief and lacked depth, marks in the highest mark bands could not be awarded. Conclusions need to include a justified answer to the question posed in the title, based on the information gathered, and where candidates scored lower marks it was due to the lack of a justified conclusion based on the evidence gathered. Most candidates showed evidence throughout their work of research undertaken which supported the information used in their assignment. Many candidates made it clear in the assignment itself where the information gathered had been used. A detailed list of sources attracted high marks for research where it was clear what information has been gathered and how the information had been used to answer the coursework title. Appropriateness of assessment tasks Most candidates had a clearly stated question at the beginning of their assignment and these were questions that encouraged analysis and evaluation of the data collected and resulted in high marks being awarded. Feasibility studies for setting up a new business continued to be the most popular focus for assignments. These allowed both breadth and depth to the research undertaken and for analysis and evaluation of this research with a clear conclusion based on the evidence gathered. Other popular areas of the syllabus content were HR/motivation and marketing. Examples of suitable assignment titles were as follows: How effective was [business name] marketing its new product/service? This question worked well when a small local business was investigated rather than a large well-known company such as McDonalds. The HR or motivation question – Is money the most important motivator? – was used successfully by several candidates. Some candidates investigated a single aspect of motivation, which worked well, e.g. How can [business name] reduce labour turnover? or How can [business name] increase efficiency or productivity? Is there scope for [type of business] in [name of town]? or Would [name of town] be a good location to set up a [type of business]? or Is there a market gap for a [type of business]? This is always a good topic to select because candidates choose a type of retailer or business in which they are interested and they are familiar with the area in which they are going to locate it. This usually results in a good evaluation as well as a well-researched piece of coursework. Candidates usually produce plenty of primary and secondary information and write up their assignment including analysis and evaluation of the data gathered, so gaining high marks. The conclusion usually fully justifies the recommendation as to whether or not the business should be set up using the evidence gathered.
